By the end of 2023, RNG projects produced an estimated 108 TBtu (Argonne National Laboratory 2025). While the majority of RNG is used for transportation, a portion is also used by utilities or private entities. Additional uses being investigated in the United States and abroad include as a direct substitute for liquefied natural gas as a maritime fuel, and as a feedstock to produce SAF via gas-to-liquids pathways (e.g., SkyNRG’s Project Wigeon [SkyNRG n.d.]). 2.9 Marine and Rail Biofuels The International Organization for Standardization 8217:2024 specification for marine fuels was adopted in 2024 enabling the use of up to B100 in nearly every grade of marine fuel applications (both distillates and residual fuel). Marine biofuel feedstocks under consideration include forestry and agricultural residues; energy crops; waste oils, fats, and greases; manure; sewage sludge; landfill gas; algae; and municipal solid wastes. Biofuels accounted for about 1% of global marine fuel use in 2024 based on fuel sampling representative of 65 million metric tons (Bee 2025). Multiple marine biofuels are being considered, and a multi-fuel future is anticipated. Drop-in fuels would require minimal changes prior to use in existing engines and infrastructure. These include namely renewable diesel and biodiesel, with bio-crude and bio-oil also being investigated. Liquefied RNG, referred to in the maritime industry as bio-liquefied natural gas, is also considered a drop-in substitute for liquefied natural gas within the existing natural gas fleet. Emerging non-drop-in fuels include bio-methanol and lignin-alcohol mixes.
